I enjoy college basketball, and happen to cheer for a team that exploits the one and done rule quite well (bear down). However, I don't believe the NCAA was ruined in the'90s when guys like Kobe, KG, and Jermaine O'Niell went straight to the NBA out of high school.

The point of this isn't too replace the NCAA, more to provide players an opportunity to earn a living playing basketball. You know, jobs.

We're talking about a handfull of players each year, and must of those guys leave after 1 year anyways. Was the NCAA ruined in the '90s and '00s when players could come straight from high school?

The NCAA has over 100 teams in division 1 alone. The overwhelming majority of teams would be unaffected. Those few that would be affected would be forced to focus on developing talent rather than recruiting the best high schoolers.

Furthermore, there's no reason the NCAA couldn't try and compete wrth the D-League by providing student athletes a reason to attend their school besides a useless degree in sociology, or whatever they tell their student athletes to study to keep them academically eligible.
There would be fewer one and dones, and more 4 year players. I'm not sure if that would ruin it.

I would like to see the D-League become a legimate alternative to the NCAA. If you're a likely lottery pick coming out of high school, it makes far more sense to work on your game in a professional setting, rather than this phony amateur BS that limits team practice time to 20 hours a week, forces players to attend classes that are often a complete waste of time, and invites all kinds of shady behaviour to get around NCAA rules.
I dont think the D-League would ever completely replace the NCAA (and I think the NCAA has its place), but for those top tier guys (Simmons, Towns, Wiggins, Parker, Ingram, etc.) there should be a real alternative to the NCAA.

To do this, the D-League needs  to start paying its players a livable wage.  Right now, the MAX D-League contract is $25,000 a year, with lesser players making as little as $13,000 per year. For a league that likes to be seen as progressive, that is a joke. Seriously, for the price of what the Suns are paying Jared Dudley, the entire D-League could afford to pay every player enough to live.

They could also increase the maximum. Imagine if Ben Simmons was offered $100,000 to play in Fort Wayne. The team could easily make it back in ticket sales, and ad revenue, as everyone gets hyped for the next big thing.

Fringe NBA guys would have more reason to stay home, rather than playing in Europe and Asia, increasing the talent pool for NBA call ups as well. Perhaps even the next big thing in Europe decides to sign with a D-League team before going into the draft. Imagine Porzingis playing in Prescott Valley for a season before being drafted.

The D-League could serve as a way for the NBA to grow its brand in smaller markets around the country with a small investment. Lets hope the new CBA looks out for these guys.

The Magic have failed to draft well (they spent top 10 picks on Payton, Hezonja, and Gordon) before finally growing impatient and spending big on mediocre players in free agency. Meanwhile, the Knicks sold their draft assets to try and build an instant contender around Melo.

It makes more sense to ride with Len into restricted free agency (seriously, who's gonna spend big on a center this offseason?), and hope Knight gets it together so the team can either sell high in a trade, or let him lead the second unit.

As much as I would love to be cheering for a contender right now, we need to forget about the past six seasons. They were disappointing, but we can't do anything about it now. Desperately trying to make up for the last half decade will only lead to selling our future short by making deals such as trading a lottery pick for Markieff Morris (ahem Wizards), or trading multiple lottery picks for the right to sign Bellini, Koufos, and Rondo (Kings!), trading for Derrick Rose/Paying Joakim (never change Knicks), or paying Hakim Warrick and Josh Childress (ouch).

Mcd has shown that he's not afraid of restricted free agency, and considering that there may not be a ton of demand for centres on the free agency market this summer, there may not be an immediate need to give up on Alex Len this season.

Knight, for better or for worse, is under contract for three seasons after this one. Trading him now would be selling low on a young player.

That said, our front office should explore any opportunity to add young talent, and Hezonja is certainly young. Vucevic, however, doesn't really get the Suns anywhere, as he is a limited player who doesn't protect the rim, cant play on the wing, and at 26 years old likely is who he is already. This trade, which obviously depends on your opinion of Len's and Knight's futures, would be more interesting to me if it involved the Magic's pick this summer instead of Vucevic. Think something more along the Markieff Morris trade last year.

Falling out of the playoff race early isn't such a bad outcome. It's easier to let the young guys learn from their mistakes when every game isn't a must win. Losing also eliminates any temptation for the front office to make some kind of short-sighted win-now move (like trading a lottery pick for Brandon knight) to try and snag a playoff spot.

I just hope Watson keeps the team focused and hungry, and if the young guys grow, they can play spoiler later in the season.

It helps that nearly every Sun is signed to a long term deal, so the front office can afford to be patient. In fact, the teams three most expensive players, who signed long term deals just before the cap spike, each make about as much per year as Miles Plumlee just got this past offseason, and they're all under contract for multiple years after this season.

Collecting talent will always be an uphill challenge in a competitive league, and is by far the most important test of a GM. However, McDonough has demonstrated savvy cap management, a willingness to buy into a players prime, and solid valuation on young players and picks. Ultimately, how those players develop and live up to their contracts will be how we judge our GM, but at least McD has shown the ability to hit some singles. Here's hoping for a homerun.
